The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Unilever (ULVR-GB): a better business at a fair price, whose earnings per share stand still until FY2029 and whose published estimates must fall first

26-Nov-2026. Share price 4,887.5p (20-Nov-2026). Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, model update 2. Money is in euros unless stated. Negative numbers are shown in brackets.

Two terms used throughout. "The continuing business" is what Unilever keeps once Foods has been combined with McCormick: home care, personal care, beauty and wellbeing, plus the foods retained in India, Nepal and Portugal. "With Foods" is today's perimeter, which every published broker forecast still uses for FY2027 and FY2028. The basis of the figures, two corrections to the source reports and the checks made are in Appendix A at the end.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one sentence. Unilever is a good business that is getting better, at a fair price; its improvement will not reach earnings per share for about two years, and its published estimates must fall before they can rise.
Verdict

A sound case, fairly priced, without the positive skew that Richard looks for. The case becomes one of his setups if Unilever passes the three 2027 tests while its share price falls on the mechanical restatement of estimates.

€3.21 to €3.16the model's earnings per share, FY2026 to FY2028: flat, before growth of 6% to 7% a year resumes in FY2029
(10)% to (15)%expected cut to published consensus FY2028 earnings per share during 2027, about two-thirds of it Foods leaving
19.04xguideline fair multiple: the middle of the ten-year range once earnings are put on one basis
+12.0%total return to 31-Dec-2027 at the guideline multiple; about +7% once weighted for the bad case
20% to 25%chance that developed-market volume breaks and forces a margin reset
1The business is improving, and the improvement is real. Under a chief executive appointed in March 2025, Unilever has demerged Ice Cream, agreed to combine Foods with McCormick, finished a cost programme early and delivered its best volume growth in more than a decade. The company that remains is the world's second-largest home and personal care company, and it is strongest in emerging markets, where most of the growth is. On this point I agree with the market.
2Earnings per share stand still until FY2029, for mechanical reasons. The model has earnings per share of €3.21 in FY2026 and €3.16 in FY2028, followed by growth of 6% to 7% a year. Three effects that have little to do with trading offset three years of operating growth: the Foods cash goes mainly to tax and debt, which earn far less than the profit sold; currency translation costs about 2% of sales a year; and Foods leaves shared costs behind on the continuing business. The business is not deteriorating; the shareholder's benefit is deferred.
3Published estimates must fall, so upgrades cannot drive the shares for 12 to 18 months. Every published forecast still contains Foods. As brokers remove Foods during 2027, consensus FY2028 earnings per share should fall by 10% to 15%, and about two-thirds of that fall is a change of perimeter that alters no value. Even so, upgrades to guidance and estimates, which are the usual engine of outperformance and Richard's central test, are unavailable for 12 to 18 months, and on data screens the restatement will look like a wave of downgrades.
4The shares are fairly priced: neither the bargain nor the premium that the screens show. One share price gives three multiples: about 16 times published earnings with Foods, which looks cheap; about 17 times our own forecast with Foods; and about 18½ times the continuing business's earnings, which looks dear. On one consistent basis the shares sit near the middle of their ten-year range, and the guideline fair multiple of 19.04x is that same middle, expressed on the new perimeter.
5The expected return is respectable but not skewed. At the guideline multiple the model gives a total shareholder return of +12.0% to 31-Dec-2027 and +24.6% to 30-Jun-2029, or 9% to 11% a year. Dividends and the roll-forward of the valuation year to FY2029 make almost all of that return; the multiple adds almost nothing.
6One operating risk is real: developed-market volume under the 2027 price increases. Developed-market volume is already falling before the 2027 price increases arrive, and competitors are pricing below what Unilever needs. I put the chance of a volume break that forces a margin reset, as happened at Haleon, Reckitt and Beiersdorf in 2026, at 20% to 25%. A reset of that kind would cost about 8.5% of FY2028 earnings per share before any fall in the multiple.
7The order of events matters: good news comes first and the tests come later. The next four to six months should bring a delivered FY2026, progress on United Kingdom clearance of the Foods deal and a 2027 guide on the usual framework. The three tests follow: first-quarter volume (late April 2027), the first-half margin (late July 2027) and the first half-year without Foods (reported February 2028). Good news before the tests is not evidence that the thesis is proving itself.
8Two developments together would turn this fair case into one of Richard's setups. The first is the 2027 tests passed; the second is the restatement of estimates behind us. From about mid-2028 the company is simpler, its balance sheet is under-used, the savings are flowing and earnings per share are growing again. A share price that falls along the way for mechanical reasons would add the positive skew that is missing today.

Five judgements move the value of the shares most over the next one to two years (each is sized in #9): (1) developed-market volume under the 2027 price increases; (2) currency; (3) how much of the savings shareholders keep; (4) what the Foods cash is worth after tax, and how Unilever uses it; and (5) the multiple the market pays once the restated earnings are visible.

Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. All scores are set by the Rater.

#1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

The operating environment turns from a tailwind into a moderate headwind in 2027: sales growth holds, but margin and volume lose the help they had in 2026.

Evidence

  • Demand has split in two. In the third quarter of 2026 emerging markets (about 60% of sales) grew underlying sales by 9.5%, with volume up 6.0%. Developed markets shrank by 0.9%, with volume down 1.7%.
  • Part of the emerging-market strength is borrowed. India's sales-tax cut of September 2025 drops out of the comparison from the fourth quarter of 2026, and Brazil's tax reform causes destocking in the same quarter. Stripped of these two effects, emerging markets are growing at about 6% to 7%.
  • Input costs have turned against Unilever more than against its peers. The company guides 2027 net material inflation at 1.3% to 1.8% of the continuing business's sales. Unilever is the most exposed of its peers because its costs lean on crude-oil derivatives, palm oil and packaging: Morgan Stanley estimates 3.1% of sales over 2025 to 2027 for Unilever, against 0.9% to 1.9% for L'Oréal, Reckitt and Beiersdorf.
  • Scanner data are weakening before Unilever's 2027 price increases land: volume is (3.9)% in the United States and (4.7)% in Western Europe (chart above).
  • The emerging-market growth engine is already paying for its volume. Hindustan Unilever, the listed Indian subsidiary, grew sales 15% in the September quarter, but its gross margin fell by 397 basis points and it cut advertising by 9%.

InferenceEvery favourable condition of the eighteen months to mid-2026 is unwinding within two or three quarters. Those conditions were falling input costs, easy comparisons, a tax stimulus in India and stumbling competitors.

Sales growth will hold at 4% to 5% because price takes over from volume, but price that only recovers cost earns nothing extra. The sector's rule of thumb (Deutsche Bank) is that volume growth falls below 2% once price rises above 2.5%, and the 2027 forecast needs price of about 2.6%.

The emerging-market engine also converts into euro earnings at well under one for one, a link that brokers rarely draw. The inflation that produces local price growth also produces currency devaluation, and India's success raises the share of profit that belongs to the 38% minority shareholders in Hindustan Unilever.

So whatThe 2027 environment does not threaten Unilever's sales line. It removes the help that margin and volume enjoyed in 2026, and it does so in the year when the company's own changes are most demanding. That combination is why the forecast has no margin gain in 2027.

Where I differ from the market

Every broker's note centres on the 2027 trade-off between price and volume, and I agree with that framing. I differ on two points. I treat currency as a standing cost of about 2% of sales a year, where most brokers model today's exchange rates and so assume none. And I read Hindustan Unilever's falling gross margin as an early warning for the group, a signal that is absent from the group debate.

Counter-case

2027 may prove an ordinary year. Deutsche Bank notes that falling crude and palm oil prices point to less cost growth than feared. At today's exchange rates the currency drag in the first half of 2027 would be close to nil. And Walmart has so far let suppliers raise prices.

What would change my view

A first-quarter 2027 statement (late April 2027) showing continuing-business volume growth of 2% or more, with price of 2.5% or more and developed-market volume no worse than (2)%. Earlier, Hindustan Unilever's December-quarter results (January 2027) with a gross margin that is no longer falling by hundreds of basis points.

Conclusion: The environment is turning from a tailwind into a moderate headwind for 2027, so this topic's test of strong or improving tailwinds is not met, although the headwinds are known, dated and of manageable size.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. The structural emerging-market engine (about 60% of sales, 6-7% underlying once the India tax cut and Brazil destocking are stripped out) is real, but over 2027-28 it is outweighed by dated external headwinds on the base case: net material inflation of 1.3-1.8% of sales with Unilever the most exposed peer, developed-market competitors and private label pricing below what it needs, scanner volumes already (3.9)% in the US and (4.7)% in Western Europe, and a standing currency cost of about 2% of sales; consensus sales growth at the 32nd percentile fits, and sales hold only because price replaces volume. A slightly negative balance of real structural tailwinds against known, dated threats sits in the low 40s, coherent with the group's 38 but a little above it because the headwinds are of manageable size and the emerging-market leg is widening; just below Carlsberg's modest mature environment and above Entra's.

#2Internally driven corporate change

Unilever's internal change is top-quartile and largely delivered, but its largest step, the Foods transaction, dilutes earnings per share before it helps, and the benefit arrives only in FY2029.

Evidence

InferenceThis is a top-quartile programme of change for a large consumer staples company: broad, funded, and run by a team that has been given no room for excuses. Two features decide what the programme is worth to a shareholder over the next two years.

First, the Foods transaction dilutes earnings per share before it helps. The Foods cash goes mostly to separation taxes and to debt reduction, and both return far less than the profit sold. Even after a share consolidation matched to value, earnings per share lose about 9%. Had the net cash bought back shares instead, the loss would have been about 4%. Choosing debt reduction therefore costs about 5% of earnings per share, and in return leverage falls to about 1.3 to 1.5 times EBITDA, against the company's stated comfort range of 1.8 to 2.0 times.

Second, 2027 stacks three changes on one another: a separation, a re-organisation and a year of rising input costs. The precedents point both ways, and Unilever's 2027 conditions resemble Haleon's more than Procter & Gamble's.

Procter & Gamble, 2019

  • Re-organised
  • Then posted its best quarter in 13 years

Haleon, 2026: closer to Unilever's 2027

  • Moved to regional units in January 2026
  • Cut guidance within the year

So whatThe change forces are strong enough to trust the continuing business, but they do not produce a step-up in earnings per share within Richard's window of 12 to 24 months. The step-up arrives in FY2029, when the left-behind costs have been removed and the balance sheet can be put to work.

Where I differ from the market

Every broker tells the story of a pure home and personal care company, and I agree with its direction and with the quality of execution. I differ on a number that no broker states: the dilution that remains after the share consolidation. Brokers present the consolidation as the cure for the dilution, but the consolidation cures only the part that is matched by McCormick shares handed to holders.

Counter-case

Procter & Gamble shed 60% of its brands between 2014 and 2019, kept investing, then led its sector on growth and was re-rated. That is the template, and Unilever is following it faster. Procter & Gamble took about five years, starting from a stronger position in the United States.

What would change my view

A decision to use the spare balance sheet for buybacks, most likely after the one-year lock-up on the McCormick stake ends in mid-2028. A numerical margin target for the continuing business. A first half under the regional model without loss of developed-market share.

Conclusion: Internal change forces are strong, broad and well resourced, but they carry real problems in 2027, and their benefit to earnings per share is deferred to FY2029.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. A broad, funded reset is largely delivered and visibly working: Ice Cream demerged, Foods agreed to McCormick for $15.7bn plus shares, brands cut from about 370 to 180, the €800m programme finished early with a new €1bn to 2029, about 90% of the executive team replaced with pay on growth, cash and return on invested capital, and 2026 brought the best volume in over a decade and two guidance raises. It is held below 75 by internal problems: the chosen use of the Foods cash dilutes earnings per share about 9% (5 points of it from preferring debt reduction), 2027 stacks a separation on the third organisational design in five years (the Haleon precedent), US wellbeing is declining, and the earnings payoff waits until FY2029; I sit a touch above the group's 70, between Instalco's working turnaround and Theon's deliberate pivot.

#3Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Unilever's foundations are sound and one notch below the sector's best: its advantages protect the emerging-market growth engine better than the developed-market profit pool.

Evidence

  • Position. About 90% of home and personal care revenue comes from first or second positions in a country and category, and 35 such positions supply more than half of sales.
  • Advantage and structure. Unilever's strongest advantage, distribution in emerging markets, is widening; its brand advantage in developed markets is narrowing. The industry structure splits the same way.
  • Pricing power only recovers cost. Unilever recovers cost increases with a lag of 12 to 24 months and pays for the recovery in volume: in 2023 European price rose 12.8% and volume fell 7.7%.
  • Management is decisive, but untested in a year of rising input costs. The team is fast and unusually open about the building blocks of its plan. Its goals stretch: volume growth above 2% a year, where the company managed under 1% a year over the previous decade. The team has not yet managed a full year of rising input costs, the kind of year in which Unilever's record is weakest (2022: operating margin down 230 basis points). After three organisational designs and large role cuts, the culture is in transition, not settled.
  • Capital allocation is steady, not dynamic. The buyback runs at €1.5bn a year whatever the share price, and the United States wellness acquisitions have disappointed.

InferenceUnilever is an above-average business: high returns, low cyclicality, strong cash generation and leading positions. It sits a notch below the best for three reasons: it has turned scale into profit less well than Procter & Gamble, its pricing power only recovers cost, and it is slowly losing share in developed markets. The company that remains after Foods is better on growth, gross margin and focus.

So whatFoundations of this quality support a mid-range multiple or better and make a fundamental collapse unlikely. They do not, by themselves, produce upgrades.

Where I differ from the market

I agree that the continuing business deserves a premium to Reckitt and Haleon. I disagree with two comfortable beliefs. Cash conversion is not 100% for the shareholder. And the retained Magnum and McCormick stakes are not spare money for extra buybacks: they are already needed to fund the present level of returns. The resource that really is spare is the balance sheet.

Counter-case

The margin gap to peers is an opportunity as well as a weakness. Deutsche Bank sees long-term upside to an operating margin of 22% to 23%, and the overhead base from which to improve is soft: overheads rose about 35% between 2021 and the start of the current programme.

What would change my view

A gross margin that rises through 2027 despite inflation. Developed-market share that holds through the price increases.

Conclusion: A favourable structure in the core categories, a real and widening advantage in emerging markets, an above-average financial profile and a decisive management team add up to sound foundations, one notch below the best in the sector.

Score: 69, set by the Rater. Qualitatively above average: number one or two positions for about 90% of home and personal care revenue, concentrated and rational laundry and cleaning, a widening emerging-market distribution moat (nine million outlets in India), very low cyclicality and high predictability; against that, pricing power only recovers cost, developed-market brand share is slipping (US deodorant 44% to 40%) and culture is in transition. The figures confirm a good, not elite, profile (return on invested capital 13.5% at the 79th percentile, gross margin 73rd, operating margin 69th; the 36% free cash conversion understates the 80-88% after restructuring), and the continuing business is better on growth and gross margin; I sit above the groups' 58-64 because they underweight predictability and the improving perimeter, just below Tele2's recurring oligopoly and above Carlsberg's comparable staples franchise.

#4Conservatism of guidance and the record of delivery

Guidance is realistic, not conservative: this team's record of beating sales guides is good, but in 2027 the forecast sits at the bottom edge of every guided range.

Evidence

  • The record under this management is good. Volume guidance was raised twice in 2026. Third-quarter underlying sales growth was 5.2% against 4.8% expected, and first-half earnings per share were €1.61 against €1.59 expected. The medium-term sales range was itself raised from 3% to 5%.
  • In years of rising costs, sales beats came with price, lower margins and falling volume. Sales growth far exceeded the opening guide in 2022 (9.0% against 4.5% to 6.5%) and in 2023 (7.0% against 3% to 5%).
  • Management's informal comment is more cautious than its formal guidance. Management says that India is "not naturally a 15% growth" business, that wellbeing recovers only in the second half of 2027, and that the response of volume to price in 2027 is unknown.

InferenceGuidance is realistic, not conservative. The habit of raising guidance is genuine for sales and volume and absent for margin. A sales "raise" in 2027, if it is made with price, would not be good news for earnings.

The basis of the 2027 sales guide will decide whether it is met. In the third quarter of 2026 the continuing business grew 6.9% and the group 5.2%, because Foods grew 0.1%. The range of 4% to 6% is therefore easy for the continuing business and hard for the group. On the forecast, the continuing business grows about 4.0% in the first half of 2027 and the group with Foods about 3¼%. If the guide is given for continuing operations, which I think likely, the forecast is inside the range. If the guide is given for the group, a first-half miss is the central case. Richard should check the basis of the guide on 11-Feb-2027 before reading the number.

So whatRichard's test of conservative guidance is half met. Management keeps expectations in check informally, which is a good habit, but the formal ranges leave no cushion in 2027.

Where I differ from the market

Consensus takes the 2027 volume framework at face value (2.0%); I am a little below it, at 1.7%. I agree with the market that FY2026 will be delivered.

Counter-case

This team has beaten every sales guide it has given, and its informal caution may be the preparation for further beats.

What would change my view

A 2027 guide on 11-Feb-2027 that is given for continuing operations, with volume of "at least 2%" and margin improvement stated without qualification, followed by first-quarter volume at or above that level.

Conclusion: The record of delivery and of raising sales guidance is good, but current guidance is realistic rather than conservative, and it is exposed at its lower end in 2027.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. Under this management the record is good on sales and volume: volume guidance raised twice in 2026, third-quarter underlying sales growth 5.2% against 4.8% expected, first-half earnings per share a small beat, the medium-term range raised, and every opening sales guide since 2022 beaten, with informal commentary kept below consensus; but the 2022-23 beats were made with price at lower margins, there is no margin number to beat, and current guidance is realistic rather than conservative, with the forecast at the bottom edge of every 2027 range and a first-half miss the central case if the guide is set for the group. I sit above the groups' 48 and 42 because the formal record has no miss and informal caution is a good habit, but below MITIE's continuing upgrade record and above Renew, which did cut.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost control and feedback loops

Unilever's operating leverage works only on volume, and most of its savings will not reach the shareholder, so revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth only in volume-led years; 2027 is not one.

Evidence and reasoning

  • Operating leverage exists only on volume. The company states a marginal contribution of 60% to 65% on extra volume. Because brand and marketing investment is managed as a share of sales, some of that contribution is re-spent. Price that only recovers cost adds nothing. 2026 was the exception (first-half volume up 4.2%), and 2027 reverses it.
  • Most of the savings do not reach the shareholder. Of the €1bn of gross savings, I expect about €450m to €500m to remove the costs left behind by Foods, about €400m to €450m to be reinvested, and only €100m to €150m (about 0.3% of sales) to be kept as margin. On the company's figures, productivity capital spending adds 20 to 30 basis points of gross margin a year, about half of that after the extra depreciation.
  • Reinvestment is a choice, and newer evidence makes it look less forced. The Capital Markets Day slides show the continuing business already investing more than 18% of sales in its brands, as a present level rather than a target; the 16.1% reported is for the group with Foods. I hold the 18% figure with medium confidence, because it has not been reconciled with the chief executive's own remark of "16%". On definitions that are not fully comparable, 18% is above Procter & Gamble, Colgate and Reckitt and below Haleon and L'Oréal (chart below). The forecast still assumes that roughly one further point of sales is reinvested by 2030. That assumption is fair, because management says it will put growth first, but it is also the one place where the forecast could prove too cautious in 2029 and 2030.
  • Financial leverage is being reduced, so it works against earnings per share (see #2).
  • Feedback loops run both ways, and their timing differs. The balancing loops all peak in 2027. From 2028 the reinforcing loops modestly dominate.

Reinforcing loops: modestly dominate from 2028

  • Savings fund brand investment, which drives volume, which absorbs fixed cost
  • Distribution and data in emerging markets compound

Balancing loops: all peak in 2027

  • Price widens the gap to private label and costs developed-market volume
  • Competitors reinvest the gains from their own margin resets
  • Currency and minority interests tax emerging-market growth
  • The re-organisation distracts management

InferenceIn a normal year after the transition, the chain from sales to earnings is short and unexciting. In FY2029 the model has reported sales up 3.1%, operating profit up 5.8% and earnings per share up 6.9%. Earnings per share therefore grow about twice as fast as reported sales, and about half of that gearing comes from savings that are finite.

So whatRichard's test is that revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth. Unilever met that test in 2026, will not meet it in 2027 or 2028, and meets it modestly from 2029.

Where I differ from the market

The market's narrative for 2028 and 2029 is "compounding": Deutsche Bank writes of high single-digit growth in earnings per share. I have 6% to 7%. The difference is small, and it is unfavourable.

Counter-case

The marginal contribution is high, so every point of volume above plan is worth far more than a point of sales (about 2.4% of earnings per share; see #9). Volume and mix have averaged 2.7% over the last eleven quarters. If that rate persists through 2027, the leverage is real and the forecast is too low.

What would change my view

Brand investment held flat as a share of sales while volume growth stays at 2% or more, which would show that Unilever can keep its savings.

Conclusion: The business model has real leverage on volume and credible scope to cut cost, but its pricing power only recovers cost and its financial leverage is being reduced, so revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth only in volume-led years, and 2027 is not one.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. The structure has one strong gear and three weak ones: a 60-65% marginal contribution on extra volume (each point of volume is about 2.4% of earnings per share), but pricing power that only recovers cost with a 12-24 month lag (2023 Europe price +12.8%, volume (7.7)%), financial leverage being cut to 1.3-1.5x, and of the €1bn gross savings only about €100-150m likely kept as margin after stranded costs and reinvestment. Reinforcing loops (savings into brands into volume, emerging-market distribution scale) dominate only from 2028, and in FY2029 earnings per share grow about twice reported sales, the Universe median ratio; asymmetric leverage on volume without pricing power is the ordinary mix, a little below Carlsberg's 57, coherent with the Economic strength group's 63 and the Financial forecasts group's 33 on either side.

#6Forecast financials

The model's earnings per share go sideways to FY2028 and grow 6% to 7% a year only from FY2029, so there is no scope for double-digit growth; about two-thirds of the gap to consensus is simply Foods leaving.

Evidence: the model's forecasts

FY2025 earnings per share is the actual on the brokers' basis. The model's FY2027 earnings per share is flattered by about €0.15 by the timing of the share consolidation (Appendix A), so the row on average shares is the better guide for FY2027. The model's FY2027 free cash flow includes about €1.6bn of working capital that leaves with Foods, which is a transfer inside the transaction, not an operating outflow.

InferenceThe table carries three messages.

  1. The fall in revenue is a change of perimeter, not of trading. Foods (about €11.5bn of sales at an operating margin of about 23%) leaves in mid-2027. The continuing business grows about 3% a year in euros.
  2. The fall in margin is a change of mix plus a temporary cost. A higher-margin business leaves, and €400m to €500m of shared costs land on the continuing business before the savings remove them. The company's pro forma margin of 19.1% excludes those costs, as Bernstein and the Capital Markets Day transcript have now confirmed. From FY2029 the margin rises by 40 to 50 basis points a year.
  3. Earnings per share go sideways because gains and losses cancel. From FY2025 to FY2028, operating growth in constant currency adds about 14% and buybacks about 3%. Currency takes about 6%. The Foods exit takes 9% to 11%, because the cash goes to tax and debt and the left-behind costs are not yet removed. Minority interests and tax take about 2%. The sum is about nil.

The gap to consensus has two parts of very different meaning. For FY2028, consensus is €3.69 and the forecast on average shares is €3.12. Our own figure with Foods still in would be about €3.52. About 5 points of the gap are therefore a real difference of view (mostly currency, with a little volume and margin), and about 11 points are simply Foods leaving.

Scope for double-digit growth: none. Earnings per share grow at about 3% a year from FY2025 to FY2030.

Scope for more growth and margin than in the past: mixed. Sales growth is similar to the last six years and of better quality from 2028, when half of it is volume. The margin gain is far smaller: about 110 basis points over five years for the continuing business, against 390 basis points for the group from FY2022 to FY2025. The earlier gain came from the cycle in input costs, and that source is exhausted.

So whatI give the operating forecast high weight: it is respectable. I give the per-share forecast medium weight: it is flat for two years, and the completion date, the consolidation ratio and the tax bill move it more than trading does.

Where I differ from the market

The forecast is not an outlier among the brokers who have done the work on the same perimeter. Jefferies' pro forma FY2027 figure before any consolidation (€2.48) is about 1% below our equivalent, and Deutsche Bank's valuation of the continuing business implies earnings 1% to 5% above ours. The difference is with the published consensus, which has not yet moved.

Counter-case

The forecast is cautious on three inputs at once: volume below the company's framework, a currency drag where today's exchange rates imply none, and the left-behind costs in full. If any one of the three proves too cautious, FY2028 earnings per share are 2% to 5% higher.

What would change my view

The company's own bridge from today's earnings to the continuing business's earnings, which may come with the FY2026 results or with the shareholder circular.

Conclusion: The forecasts describe a business growing underlying sales at 4% to 5% with flat earnings per share to FY2028 and growth of 6% to 7% after it, so there is no scope for double-digit growth and far less margin gain than in the past three years.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Growth of nil to 5% gives D; the low figure is mainly a perimeter effect (Foods cash going to tax and debt, stranded costs, about 2% a year of currency) offsetting about 14% constant-currency operating growth to FY2028, with 6-7% earnings-per-share growth only from FY2029. I place it a little below mid-band because the growth that does come is organic and better in quality (half volume from 2028), but the margin path (19.3% to 20.2%) adds about 110bps over five years against 390bps in FY2022-25, so it does not beat the past.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

On Richard's central test the answer for the next 6 to 12 months is no: published estimates must fall, and like-for-like estimates lean mildly negative. The scope for upgrades reopens from about mid-2028.

Evidence: guidance

Across 2027 as a whole, a softening of guidance is about twice as likely as a raise (30% against 15%).

Evidence: estimatesPublished estimates have three layers, and the layers should not be added together.

1. FY2026 estimates are in line.

No change is likely.

2. Like for like, FY2027 and FY2028 estimates are 2% to 5% too high.

Until February the drift is nonetheless upward, because brokers model today's exchange rates: consensus FY2027 earnings per share rose 1%, 1% and 2% over the last one, three and six months.

3. The restatement is certain in direction, and Unilever chooses how large it looks.

Brokers will move to the continuing business one by one between February and August 2027, and for some months the FactSet average will mix two perimeters and mean nothing. I put the chance that the FactSet average for FY2028 is more than 10% lower in nine months at 55%, and the chance that it is 3% to 10% lower at 30%. Each point of the consolidation ratio moves every per-share figure by 1.2% and changes no value.

Evidence: narrativeThe favourable half of the story is fully told. The unfavourable half is told in pieces by different houses, and no house combines the two halves into the view here.

HouseThe half of the story it tellsStance
Deutsche BankThe perimeter and the multiple right; assumes no currency dragBuyer
JefferiesThe volume risk, the currency and the left-behind costsSeller
This memoBoth halves: "operations fine, earnings per share flat for two years, price fair"Fair

InferenceRichard's central test asks whether the chance of upgrades to guidance and estimates is unusually skewed to the positive. For the next 6 to 12 months the answer is no. The skew is negative on published numbers and mildly negative like for like.

So whatThree facts soften that answer, and the third is an opportunity.

  1. Most of the cut is appearance, and the specialists who set the price already describe it as such.
  2. Ratings have room to rise. Only 25% of analysts rate the shares a buy, and target prices are not mechanically affected by the restatement, because brokers value the continuing business and the McCormick shares separately.
  3. The gap closes on known dates, and the balance then turns positive. From about mid-2028 the earlier research puts the chance that the savings programme is raised at 25% to 30%, that buybacks are raised at 25%, and that "modest improvement" is replaced by a numerical margin target at 30%.
25-30%chance the savings programme is raised, from about mid-2028
25%chance buybacks are raised
30%chance of a numerical margin target
25%of analysts rate the shares a buy today: room to rise

Where I differ from the market

Data screens will read the restatement as a wave of downgrades, and specialists will look through it. I side with the specialists that the restatement changes no value. I differ from them in thinking that the like-for-like numbers are also a little too high.

Counter-case

The restatement may clear the air. Once estimates are on the continuing business and carry the left-behind costs, revisions can only improve, and a simpler company may attract buyers who would not own the conglomerate.

What would change my view

Brokers moving early to the continuing business at or above the figures here. Currencies flat through the first half of 2027. A 2027 guide that is raised during the year on volume, not on price.

Conclusion: There is no scope for published upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months, because the published numbers must fall, and only a modest chance of upgrades like for like; the scope reopens from about mid-2028.

Score: 26, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, leans to softening about two to one over 2027 (30% against 15%), with the 2027 ranges giving no cushion; consensus FY2027-28 is 2-5% too high like for like (about (0.5) to (1.1) times the 4-5% revenue growth rate), on top of a value-neutral restatement that will read as a 10-15% cut to FY2028 on screens, and the near-term drift up (+1%/+2%, 55th-56th percentile) rests on stale currency assumptions. Only the narrative has room, with Buy ratings at the 13th percentile and specialists looking through the restatement; so revisions lean negative, below Indutrade where downgrades and upgrades are equally likely and above Xvivo's deeper downgrade risk, and below the group's 33 because guidance and like-for-like consensus both point down.

#8Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative, share price and peers

Momentum today is good in estimate revisions, neutral in the share price and weak among peers, and the good part will reverse mechanically during 2027.

EvidenceThe dashboard's pinned ratings, from its snapshot of 23-Nov-2026:

Sell-side earnings momentumB Thematic momentumA Technical momentumC ValuationB
  • Estimate momentum is the best in the sector. The dashboard's revision-momentum score for Unilever is 13, the best of the six stocks in its sector (chart below). The share of buy ratings has risen four points in three months, helped by Deutsche Bank's upgrade to Buy on 10-Nov-2026.
  • The share price has recovered, but its trend is barely rising. The price is 5% above its 200-day average, but that average has risen in only three of the last twelve months, and relative strength is at the 50th percentile of the universe. Price returns:
+2%3 months
+13%6 months
(10.5)%9 months
about nil12 months
  • Peers' momentum is weak. Technical momentum is C or D for every peer except L'Oréal (B), and sell-side momentum is D or F for every peer except L'Oréal (A).
  • The recent re-rating was the sector's, not Unilever's. European consumer staples re-rated by about 12% in October 2026 as investors moved from technology into defensive shares. Unilever's correlation with its peer basket is 0.76, the highest in two years, with a beta of 0.94. Over six months the shares beat the basket by only 1.5 points, although Unilever was the only company in the group to raise guidance.

InferenceMomentum in estimates is real, modest and relative: Unilever is the best house in a weak street. Momentum in the share price is neutral and borrowed from the sector. Momentum in the narrative is positive but contested. On the positive side are the Capital Markets Day and the Deutsche Bank upgrade. On the contested side, Jefferies rates the shares Underperform, a long-standing holder sold out and criticised the Foods terms, and the activist investor Trian reduced its stake in November 2026.

So whatThree consequences follow.

  1. The B for sell-side momentum will not survive 2027. At the restatement every broker cuts at once, and a rating built on revisions will read as the worst in the group for reasons unrelated to trading. From then on, revisions should be read on the continuing business's operating profit.
  2. The share price is hostage to the sector. With a beta of 0.94, a 10% fall in the group takes about 9% off the shares whatever Unilever delivers.
  3. The next twelve months will be driven by company events, not the sector. The restatement, the consolidation and the distribution of McCormick shares are all company events. Around the Ice Cream demerger, the share of price variance explained by peers fell to about a quarter, so the shares' present behaviour as a sector proxy should not be assumed to continue.

Where I differ from the market

Momentum screens flatter Unilever today, and I think the most favourable of their readings, sell-side momentum, is about to become mechanical noise. I agree with the market that Unilever has the best operating momentum in European household and personal care.

Counter-case

The news of the next four to six months is likely to be good, and it could lift technical momentum from C before any test arrives.

What would change my view

The shares outperforming the peer basket on company news, with a rising 200-day average. Revisions rising on the continuing basis once brokers publish it.

Conclusion: Momentum today is good in estimate revisions, neutral in the share price and weak among peers, and the part that is good is due to reverse mechanically during 2027.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. One measure positive and the other exactly neutral is mixed, so C. Guidance was raised twice in 2026, Unilever has the best revision score in its sector, the share of Buys rose four points with Deutsche Bank's upgrade, and the price is 5% above its 200-day average with +13% over six months; but revisions are modest (+1%/+2%, about 0.3 times revenue growth), the 200-day average has risen in only three of twelve months, the rally was the sector's rotation, and peers are weak (not counted against it). That places it in the upper part of the C band, short of the contradiction that would move it to B.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Unilever is a low-risk business inside a complicated twelve-month case: most of the uncertainty is dated and mechanical, one operating risk is real at 20% to 25%, and falls of 15% to 25% in the share price are plausible on identifiable dates.

Is the case simple? As a business, yes: sales growing 4% to 5%, a slowly rising margin and a dividend yield of about 3%. As a set of published numbers, no, for about twelve months.

Three kinds of risk should be kept apart, because an analysis that mixes them will either overstate or understate the danger.

Appearance only

The completion date and the consolidation ratio move published earnings per share by several per cent and change no value.

Value, in small amounts

The tax bill on the Foods cash and the left-behind costs each move value by a few per cent.

Operating, and real

The response of developed-market volume to the 2027 price increases.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic if each is wrong. The base for the arithmetic is the model's FY2028: revenue of €43.2bn, net income of €5,614m, about 1,776m shares and earnings per share of €3.16.

1. Developed-market volume holds under the 2027 price increases (forecast: group volume +1.7% in 2027, developed markets between (1)% and nil). Each point of volume is worth 2.4% of earnings per share:

€417mof revenue: 1% of about €41.7bn of continuing sales
➜
€260mof contribution, at a marginal contribution of about 62%
➜
€185mafter about €73m of brand investment kept at 17% to 18% of sales: 2.3% of continuing operating profit
➜
€137mafter tax at 26%
➜
€0.08 a share2.4% of earnings per share
  • Plausibly wrong by 0.8 point (Jefferies forecasts 0.9%): operating profit lower by €150m and earnings per share by €0.06, or (1.9)%.
  • The bad case (20% to 25%): developed-market volume worse than (2)% for two quarters while group price runs above 3%. Peers in that position have reset their margins. A reset of 150 basis points is €650m of operating profit, €480m after tax and €0.27 a share: (8.5)% of earnings per share, before the reaction of the share price (see the precedents below).

2. Currency costs about 2% of sales a year (forecast: (2.0)% in 2027, (1.7)% a year after).

  • One point of currency is €432m of FY2028 revenue and, at the group margin, €83m of operating profit.
  • Profit falls about 1.5 times as fast as sales, because emerging-market currencies carry above-average margins and central costs are in hard currency. In the first half of 2026 currency took about 5% off sales and 6.0 points off the growth of earnings per share.
  • Each point of currency therefore costs about €125m of operating profit and about €0.05 a share: 1.5% of earnings per share.
  • If currencies stay where they are for two years, which is what most brokers model, the outcome is 3.7 points better: FY2028 earnings per share about +5.5%, or about €3.33.
  • If emerging-market currencies fall 3.5% a year, the outcome is 3.3 points worse: about (5)%, or about €3.00.

3. Shareholders keep enough of the savings for the margin to rise from FY2029 (forecast: 19.3% in FY2028, 19.8% in FY2029, 20.2% in FY2030).

  • Fifty basis points of margin on FY2029 revenue of €44.5bn is €222m of operating profit, €165m after tax and €0.09 a share: 2.8% of earnings per share.
  • If the left-behind costs last a year longer (the 2017 Spreads disposal left €250m a year for three years), FY2029 carries about €150m where the forecast has about €50m: (€100m) of operating profit, (€74m) after tax and (€0.04) a share, or (1.3)%.
  • If competitors' promotions absorb all the net savings, the FY2029 margin stays at 19.3%: (2.8)%.
  • If brand investment is held flat as a share of sales, rather than raised by about 0.3 point a year, then by FY2030 one point of sales is €459m, €340m after tax and €0.20 a share: +5.5%.

4. The Foods cash is worth about €10bn after tax and costs, and it reduces debt (forecast: about €14bn received, about €4bn of tax and costs, completion on 1-Jul-2027).

  • Each further €1bn of tax costs €40m of interest at 4%, €30m after tax and under €0.02 a share: (0.5)%. The company's envelope for tax, restructuring and separation is about €5bn, and Jefferies puts international tax alone at up to €2.7bn.
  • Moving €3bn from debt reduction to buybacks retires about 50m shares at about €60 (2.8% of the shares) and forgoes €89m of interest saved after tax (1.6% of net income): about +1%.
  • A six-month delay raises FY2027 reported earnings per share by up to 8% and changes no value.
  • Failure of the deal (5% to 10%) would raise earnings per share to about €3.35 in FY2027 and about €3.52 in FY2028, but would lose the focused company, the debt reduction and the removal of shared costs. The risk to the thesis and the risk to the earnings forecast therefore have opposite signs. On 25-Nov-2026 the United Kingdom's competition authority said it is considering McCormick's offer to sell the Colman's business, which keeps completion in mid-2027 credible; more than ten other clearances and McCormick's shareholder vote remain.

5. The market pays a mid-range multiple once the restated earnings are visible (the guideline of 19.04x at 31-Dec-2027, on two-year forward earnings per share of about €3.38).

  • One turn of the multiple is €3.38 a share: 5.3% of the value.
  • At 17.0x, the ten-year 10th percentile put on the continuing basis (see #11), the total return to 31-Dec-2027 falls from +12% to about nil.
  • At 15.8x, the equivalent of the low of March to May 2026, the return is about (6)%. Combined with the margin reset of the first judgement, it is about (14)%.

This sector punishes disappointment fast, and Unilever's own March 2026 fall shows that a low multiple is not a theoretical trough. Haleon fell 15% and Reckitt 7% on the days of their 2026 guidance cuts. Magnum, Unilever's own previous carve-out, missed consensus earnings per share by 9% at its first results and fell 16% that day, because the costs of running as two companies were not in forecasts. Kellogg lost 17% in the weeks before its 2023 separation. Unilever itself fell from 5,466p at the end of February 2026 to 4,198p at the end of March 2026, the month the Foods transaction was announced, and its multiple on published earnings fell from 18.1x to 14.1x. From today's price, a return to that multiple would be a fall of about 15%, or about 19% with a 5% cut to earnings. Jefferies' bear case is 3,600p, a fall of 26%.

The risks can be tracked well, except for one blind period in mid-2027. Almost every unknown has a date (see the timeline in #0). Two listed subsidiaries, Hindustan Unilever and Unilever Indonesia, publish quarterly margins a few weeks before the group reports, and scanner data arrive every four weeks. Against that, the group margin is seen only twice a year, and 2027 brings four changes of presentation at once: regional segments, a new accounting standard for the income statement, Foods shown as discontinued, and a new share count. For two or three months in mid-2027, year-on-year comparisons of margin and earnings per share will not be possible from published data.

Other risks.

  • Brazil tax. Brazil carries a contingent tax liability of €3.56bn that is not provisioned. It is a risk to the timing of cash and of buybacks, not to earnings in the central case.
  • The sector's rating cycle. The sector's cyclical risk is low in demand and real in rating. Historically its shares outperform while volume-led growth and rising margins coincide, and underperform once growth shifts to price and volume turns negative, as Unilever's did in 2022 and 2023. 2027 moves Unilever toward that transition, and slow growth is then punished in both earnings and the multiple.
  • The rotation that lifted the sector. The rotation into defensive shares that lifted the group in October 2026 began outside the sector, and it can reverse for reasons outside the sector.

Where I differ from the market

The market's attention is on the terms and complexity of the deal and on 2027 pricing. I agree on pricing. On the deal, I think the parameters that change only appearance receive more attention than they deserve, and the slow deterioration of developed-market volume receives a little less. My bad case is milder than Jefferies', which has a margin below 18% and a multiple below 13x.

Counter-case

The risk may be lower than I say. This management corrects commercial mistakes quickly: Brazilian laundry was mispriced in early 2025 and corrected by the third quarter, and Home Care volume grew 7.4% in the first half of 2026. A pricing error in 2027 might cost two quarters, not two years.

What would change my view

By late July 2027 the competition decision, the 2027 guide, McCormick's registration statement, the circular with the consolidation ratio and the first-half results will all have been published. If the first quarter and the first half pass without developed-market volume worse than (2)%, the riskiness of the case falls sharply.

Conclusion: This is a low-risk business inside a complicated twelve-month case: most of the uncertainty is dated, mechanical and will resolve itself, one operating risk is real at 20% to 25%, and a fall of 15% to 25% in the share price is plausible on identifiable dates.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The business is simple and low-risk (low cyclicality, leverage falling from 2.0x to 1.3-1.5x, Hindustan Unilever and scanner data giving early reads), and the next-year earnings-per-share range is moderate, about (10)% to +5% around the central case, skewed down; but for twelve months the case rests on four undisclosed deal parameters, four simultaneous presentation changes and a certain, mechanical cut to published estimates, with one real operating risk (a developed-market volume break forcing a margin reset, 20-25%, about (8.5)% of earnings per share) and sector precedents of 7-16% one-day falls. Coherent with the Risks groups' 56 and 50: better than NKT's concentrated execution risk because the drivers are dated and trackable, below Banca Generali.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Operationally the stock is reinforcing, but per share and in published numbers it is entering a stall of 12 to 18 months, before a possible second leg from FY2029.

EvidenceThe dashboard's rule gives a starting Phase of Reinforcing. The three inputs to a lifecycle judgement point in different directions.

  • Momentum: good in estimates, neutral in price, borrowed from the sector (#8).
  • Scope for upgrades: none on published numbers for 12 to 18 months (#7).
  • Risk factors: dated and mostly mechanical, with one real operating risk (#9).

InferenceTwo descriptions of the stock are both true, and they must be held together.

  • Operationally, the thesis broadened in 2026 and is being reinforced. Guidance was raised, revisions are the best in the group, and the Capital Markets Day set out the plan.
  • Per share and in published numbers, the stock is entering a stall. Earnings per share are flat for two years. The first half-year of the continuing company, reported in February 2028, is the period in which the margin dips. The favourable momentum reading reverses. And the multiple has already had the sector's re-rating.

The stock is not collapsing, because the operating engine is intact and the risks are dated. It is not turning up either, because it is not leaving a trough in fundamentals. A second leg is possible from FY2029, when earnings per share grow again, estimates can at last be compared with results, and the balance sheet has room.

So whatThe phase matters for the multiple (#11) and for patience. A stall of this kind is not a reason to doubt the business; it is a reason not to expect upgrades to pull the share price up.

Where I differ from the market

Our own earlier research, and brokers such as Redburn, treat the first report as a focused company as the step that re-rates the shares. I think that report is the one in which the dilution becomes visible, and it re-rates the shares only if the market is by then looking at FY2029.

Counter-case

The dashboard may be right. Judged by the business rather than by the share count, the continuing company is outgrowing Haleon, Reckitt and Beiersdorf by a wide margin, and if 2027 volume holds, the Reinforcing phase simply continues.

What would change my view

First-quarter and first-half 2027 results with volume growth of 2% or more would confirm Reinforcing. Developed-market volume worse than (2)% for two quarters would turn the stall into a de-rating.

Conclusion: Operationally the stock is reinforcing, but per share it is entering a stall of 12 to 18 months before a possible second leg from FY2029, so I place it at "Stalling", one step later than the dashboard's "Reinforcing".

Score: 42, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo and the computed Stalling, read as a late-Reinforcing business entering a per-share stall: operationally 2026 broadened (guidance raised, best revisions in the sector), but earnings per share are flat to FY2028, the revision reading is due to reverse mechanically in 2027, the first continuing-company half shows the margin dip, and the multiple has already had the sector's re-rating. It is not collapsing because the operating engine is intact and a second leg from FY2029 is plausible, so it sits a little above National Grid's well-known stall (better current momentum) and below Linea Directa's early turn.

#11The fair multiple

The guideline fair multiple of 19.04x is right as a centre: put on comparable earnings, it is the middle of the ten-year range, not the top decile it appears to be, and it has more room below than above during 2027.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline is 19.04x two-year forward earnings, the 90th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history, because the starting Phase is Reinforcing. The model applies the guideline to the continuing business's earnings per share at 31-Dec-2027.

My view, in three steps.

1. The headline comparison misleads in both directions. The dashboard shows a multiple of 16.2x today and says the guideline is 18% above it. But 16.2x is measured on published earnings that still contain Foods. One share price gives three readings:

Earnings usedMultiple todayHow it looks against ten years (10th percentile 15.1x, median 17.0x, 90th 19.0x)
Published consensus, with Foodsabout 16x28th percentile: cheap
Our own forecast, with Foodsabout 17xthe median: fair
The continuing business, after the consolidation (the model)18.5xnear the 90th percentile: dear

All three readings use the same price. The history was built on earnings with Foods, so only the first two rows can be compared with it.

2. Put on the same basis as the history, the guideline is a mid-range multiple, not a top-decile one. The model has the shares on 18.5x where the published figure is about 16.4x, a ratio of 1.13. The guideline of 19.04x is therefore equivalent to about 16.9x on published earnings, which is the ten-year median. Counted on average shares (Appendix A) it is nearer 16.3x, about the 35th percentile of ten years and the median of the last five. That is why the multiple contributes only +2.9% to the model's return, not 18%.

The new perimeter raises the multiple at an unchanged share price for three reasons:

  • Foods leaves at a lower effective multiple of earnings than the group's.
  • The cash reduces debt, and less-geared earnings deserve a higher multiple.
  • FY2028 earnings are temporarily depressed by the left-behind costs.

The same ratio moves the whole historical ladder. On the continuing basis the ten-year 10th percentile is about 17.0x, the median about 19.1x and the 75th percentile about 20.3x. The unadjusted ladder must not be applied to the continuing business's earnings: on that ladder 17.0x would look like the median, when on the continuing basis it is the bottom decile.

3. A mid-range multiple is right for this stock in this phase. The rule intended a top-decile multiple for a Reinforcing stock; applied to the new perimeter, it delivers a median one. I think the median is the right number, reached for a different reason: I place the stock at Stalling, and for a sound business in a stall the middle of the range is a fair centre.

The case for a higher multiple

The continuing business is better than the group that built the history: faster growth, a higher gross margin and less debt. Procter & Gamble trades on about 22 times 2028 earnings, and Unilever's long-run discount of about 15% would put the continuing business near 19x.

The case for a lower multiple

Unilever's premium of about 10% to European consumer staples excluding L'Oréal is at the top of its historical range (Deutsche Bank). Reckitt and Haleon trade on about 15x after their resets. About two turns of the present multiple came from the sector's re-rating in six months. And the 2027 tests are still ahead.

Judgement. 19.04x is a sound centre, but it is not conservative. A reasonable band for the next twelve months is about 17x to 20x on the continuing business's earnings, with more room below than above until the first quarter and first half of 2027 have passed. The upper end becomes arguable in 2028 and 2029, once earnings per share are growing again.

Where I differ from the market

Data screens say the shares are cheap. Specialists say they are fully valued: Deutsche Bank calls the premium the top of its range, and Jefferies' target implies 14.5x to 15.5x for the continuing business. I say fair, and so I differ from both.

Counter-case

Upward: focused companies have earned premium multiples, and Procter & Gamble reached about 24x after its simplification. Downward: Jefferies argues that competitive pressure in personal care, and a de-rating of the Indian subsidiary, pull the multiple down.

What would change my view

Volume growth of 2% or more through the 2027 price increases would make 20x arguable. A margin reset would make 16x to 17x the centre.

Conclusion: The guideline fair multiple of 19.04x is right as a centre, because on comparable earnings it is the middle of the ten-year range and not the 90th percentile it appears to be; it is fair rather than conservative, and it has more room below than above during 2027.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. As read the measures give cheap on one and dear on the other, C; but the own-range cheapness rests on a stale consensus that still contains Foods and is 5-14% too high, and on the memo's like-for-like basis (about 17x on its own forecast with Foods, 18.5x on the continuing business) the multiple is mid-range, so neutral on own range and dear against peers (premium at the top of its range per Deutsche Bank, two turns from the sector's re-rating) gives D, and a stalling stock does not deserve better. I place it at the top of D because the continuing business is better than the group that built the history and the memo's fair 19.04x sits slightly above today's 18.5x on that basis.

#12Total shareholder return

The return is a carry of about +12% to the end of 2027, made of dividends and the roll-forward to FY2029 earnings; weighted for the bad case it is about +7%, positive but not skewed to the upside.

Evidence: the model's return at the guideline multiple (share price £50.09 on 16-Nov-2026; the guideline is reached by 31-Dec-2027).

+10.8%a year, to 31-Dec-2027
+8.8%a year, to 30-Jun-2029

What drives each part of the return.

  • Earnings: a roll-forward, not growth. The +4.2% to the end of 2027 does not come from growth in the next twelve months' earnings, which are flat. It comes from the valuation year rolling forward, from a year that carries the dilution and the left-behind costs to FY2029, the first year of growth. This part of the return therefore depends on the market being willing, at the end of 2027, to value the shares on FY2029 earnings. Over the longer horizon, the +13.2% is growth resumed at 6% to 7% a year.
  • Dividends: the largest and most reliable part. A yield of a little over 3%, growing 3% to 4% a year, makes two-fifths of the shorter return and a third of the longer one.
  • The multiple: almost nothing, for the reason given in #11.

What the return leaves out: the McCormick shares. About 16% of a holder's value will arrive as shares in the combined McCormick company, which starts with debt of about four times EBITDA and a primary listing in the United States. European funds that cannot hold such a listing are expected to sell, as happened after the Magnum listing, although buying by United States index funds and a planned European listing should offset some of that selling. Each 10% move in the McCormick shares is 1.6 points of the holder's return.

The cone of outcomes around the point estimate (my own rough weights).

So whatThe return is a carry: dividends plus the passage of time toward FY2029. It is positive in expectation and roughly symmetric, which is not the unusual positive skew Richard looks for. Over three years the shape improves, because dividends and resumed growth accumulate while the tests of 2027 pass.

Where I differ from the market

I do not differ. The mean broker target of £52.49 is 7% above the share price and, with the dividend, gives a twelve-month return close to the model's. The range of targets is wide (Jefferies about 4,000p, Bernstein 5,800p), and that width describes the same cone.

Counter-case

If the dashboard's Phase is right and the stock deserves a top-decile multiple on comparable earnings, the fair multiple on the continuing basis is nearer 21x and the return to the end of 2027 nearer +25%. That multiple was last reached in 2019 and 2020, when interest rates were far lower.

What would change my view

A lower share price without a change in the facts, or the same share price after the April and July 2027 tests have been passed. Either would shift the weight of the cone upward.

Conclusion: A return of +12.0% to the end of 2027 and +24.6% to mid-2029 is made of dividends and the roll-forward to FY2029 earnings, with no help from the multiple; it is respectable and roughly symmetric, and it is not skewed to the upside.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. A weighted return of nil to 10% gives D; about 8% maps to about 45, made of dividends and the roll-forward to FY2029 with almost nothing from the multiple, and the three-year check (+24.6% to mid-2029, about 9% a year) is supportive. I hold it a point below because the lower tail is real (a 20-25% worse case at about (12)%, (14)% with the multiple at its 2026 low, plus deal failure) against an upside case of only about +20%.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

The business is better than the one investors have known, the case is sound but deferred, and today it fails Richard's test of unusual positive skew; a mechanical fall in the share price during 2027 could change that.

The business. Unilever after Foods is a better company than the one investors have known: faster-growing, with a higher gross margin and less debt, and led by a management team that acts. Its advantage in emerging-market distribution is real and widening. Its weaknesses are pricing power that only recovers cost, and a slow loss of volume to private label in developed markets.

The investment case. The case is sound and deferred. Three effects that have little to do with trading (the use of the Foods cash, currency and the left-behind costs) hold earnings per share flat until FY2029. Published estimates must fall by 10% to 15% during 2027. The price is fair: the middle of the stock's own range once the perimeter is put on one basis. The return on offer is the dividend plus the passage of time.

Against Richard's test. Richard looks for fundamental outcomes and upgrades that are unusually skewed to the positive. For the next 12 to 18 months Unilever's are not. The fundamental cone is roughly symmetric, with one real bad case at 20% to 25%, and the skew in published upgrades is negative, mostly for reasons of appearance.

The case is worth keeping in view because its uncertainty is unusually well dated and what lies beyond it is attractive. The dates are 11-Feb-2027, late April 2027, late July 2027 and February 2028, and most of the uncertainty is mechanical and will resolve itself. Beyond it lie a simple company, earnings per share growing 6% to 7%, an under-used balance sheet, savings that this team has a record of delivering early, and estimates that can finally be compared with results.

The setup to watch for. If the share price fell during 2027 for mechanical reasons (the restatement, the reversal of revision-based ratings, forced selling around the McCormick distribution) while developed-market volume held, the case would become "a cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a low multiple", which is one of Richard's six setups. Today that setup is not there.

The memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 53, set by the Rater. A strong, funded internal programme (72) is partly offset by an external environment turning moderately adverse in 2027 (41), and the net force does not reach per-share profits within the window: forecast earnings per share grow only about 2-3% a year (D, 36), flat to FY2028 because the Foods cash goes to tax and debt, with 6-7% growth only from FY2029. The inputs are a mild net positive with a weak and deferred financial output, so the net change sits only just above neutral, below the low-60s cases whose inputs lift profits to median growth.

Foundations' Robustness: 75, set by the Rater. Quality of 69 understates robustness on Richard's stability test: number one or two positions in concentrated core categories, non-discretionary demand, very low cyclicality, stable margins around 20%, a widening emerging-market distribution moat and leverage falling to 1.3-1.5x make collapse unlikely, as with CVS Group's stability. It is held at the floor of the band by cost-recovery pricing power, slow developed-market share loss and a delivery record (61) that is good on sales under this team but realistic rather than conservative, with margin weakest in inflationary years.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 40, set by the Rater. The case straddles two setups without fitting either: Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU (earnings-per-share upgrades) has the change (perimeter, management, cost) but in substance the change dilutes earnings per share and the step-up in earnings power is deferred beyond two years, and CfC (Cause for Concern) Clearing in a high-quality low-cyclicality business has the quality but no cause for concern yet to clear and a multiple that is mid-range, not low, on comparable earnings. Today's problems (2027 input inflation, developed-market volume, the stacked reorganisation) blur the fit further, though it is well above Shell's buyback-only case because the change mechanism is real.

Case Riskiness: 55, set by the Rater. Following topic 9 (55): a simple, low-leverage, low-cyclicality business whose risks would be paper cuts in an ordinary year, but whose next twelve months carry undisclosed deal parameters, a certain mechanical estimate cut, a 20-25% chance of a developed-market volume break with sector precedents of 15% one-day falls, and a multiple lifted by a sector rotation and dear to peers. Unlike CVS Group the multiple is not low in its range and guidance is not conservative, so it sits just above typical rather than in the 70s or 80s.

Appendix A: the basis of the figures, corrections and checks

  • The transaction assumptions. The forecasts assume that the Foods transaction completes on 1-Jul-2027 and that Unilever then consolidates its shares at about 0.84 new shares for each old one. That ratio matches the value of the McCormick shares handed to Unilever's shareholders (about 16% of today's market value), so the share price is comparable before and after the consolidation. The company has said a consolidation is expected "on or around" closing. Neither the date nor the ratio has been announced.
  • The basis of earnings per share. Earnings per share are underlying and after minority interests, the basis that brokers and the history of the multiple use. The model's FY2027 figure (€3.31) is flattered by about €0.15, because the model appears to apply half of the share consolidation six months before completion. Counted on average shares, FY2027 is about €3.15. The other years differ by 2% or less.
  • Two statements in the source reports are wrong and are not used. Management does not "target" an operating margin of 22% to 23%: that is the peer level the company showed, and its guidance remains "modest annual margin improvement". Nor does the company guide 2027 input-cost inflation of €700m to €1bn: that range is the brokers', and the company's is €550m to €750m.
  • The latest Earnings Review has been checked. It covers the half-year results to June 2026 (published 28-Jul-2026), the third-quarter trading statement (28-Oct-2026) and the Capital Markets Day (4-Nov-2026), so it matches the last period that FactSet shows as reported.
  • No forecast input has been changed. The evidence that arrived after the inputs were set (weaker scanner data, Hindustan Unilever's falling margin) moves the probability of the bad case, not the central case. The two corrections I would most like are changes to the model's mechanics, not inputs, and they have already been put to the Financial Analyst: the timing of the share consolidation inside FY2027, and a separate line for minority interests.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. The percentile ("66th percentile") is the share of the stocks scored on that item that this stock beats. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
